stops.title: What it is and why it exists
stops.contentMd:
## In one line

The EU AI Act is a risk-based EU law that sorts AI by how much harm its use could cause people (banned, high-risk, transparency-risk, minimal) and sets heavier rules the higher the risk.

## Explained simply

Think of a school playground with four kinds of games: **banned games** (pushing people off the climbing frame — never allowed), **supervised games** (the trampoline — allowed, but checked for safety, watched, and logged), **games with a sign** (the splash pool — allowed, but you must be told the floor may be wet), and **free play** (hopscotch — no rule needed).

The EU AI Act does the same for AI. A system that tricks people into harming themselves is banned. A system that decides who gets a loan or a job is the trampoline: allowed, but checked, supervised and recorded. A chatbot is the splash pool: it must tell you it's a robot. A spam filter is hopscotch.

The key idea: **the rules depend on what the AI is used for, not how clever it is.** The same face-recognition software is hopscotch when it unlocks your phone and nearly banned when police scan a crowd with it.

## Why it exists

The EU wanted two things at once: protect people's safety and fundamental rights from AI harms, and give businesses one clear rulebook instead of 27 national ones. It borrowed an idea Europe already used for toys, lifts and medical devices: prove a product is safe before it reaches the market, document how, and put a CE mark on it. High-risk AI is treated the same way — the Act reads like product-safety law because it is one.

| When | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| Apr 2021 | Commission proposes the Act; ChatGPT doesn't exist yet |
| Nov 2022 | ChatGPT launches, breaking the "risk by use" logic since one model now serves thousands of uses |
| Dec 2023 | Political deal, adding rules for general-purpose AI models |
| Jul 2024 | Published as Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 |
| Aug 2024 | Enters into force; rules switch on in stages |
| 2026 | Digital Omnibus delays high-risk rules because standards and guidance aren't ready |

It is a **regulation**, not a directive: it applies directly in every EU country without national laws copying it.
stops.artifactPrompt: In 3-4 sentences, explain the EU AI Act's risk-tiered approach to someone with no legal background, using an analogy of your own (not the playground one above). Then state one reason the Act was amended in Dec 2023 to add GPAI model rules.

stops.title: What counts as AI, who it applies to, and the risk pyramid
stops.contentMd:
## What counts as an "AI system" (Article 3)

A machine-based system that works with some autonomy and **infers** from its inputs how to produce outputs (predictions, content, recommendations, decisions) that can affect the physical or digital world. The test word is *infers*: a calculator follows fixed rules you wrote, so it isn't AI. A model that learned from data what a risky loan looks like is.

## Who it applies to

| Role | Plain meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provider | Builds the AI or sells it under their name | A fintech that builds a credit-scoring model |
| Deployer | Uses the AI in their professional work | A bank that buys that model and uses it on applicants |
| Importer, distributor | Brings it into the EU or passes it on | A reseller |
| Affected person | The human the AI is used on | The loan applicant |

Providers carry most of the duties, because they built it. Deployers carry duties about how they use it.

## Where it applies (Article 2)

It reaches outside Europe: it applies to a provider anywhere in the world that sells AI into the EU, and to a provider or deployer anywhere whose AI **output is used in the EU**. A US company scoring EU customers is in scope; a UK bank scoring UK customers is not.

**Not covered:** military and national security use, AI used only for scientific research, purely personal non-professional use, and (partly) free open-source models.

## The risk pyramid

Four tiers, widest at the bottom: **minimal risk** (most AI, no new duties) → **transparency-risk** (chatbots, deepfakes — must disclose) → **high-risk** (Annex I/III systems — heavy obligations) → **banned** (unacceptable risk, narrow list). General-purpose AI models sit outside the pyramid on their own track.
stops.artifactPrompt: Pick an AI system you've used or built (or a hypothetical one). Classify it: is it an AI system under Article 3's test? Who would be the provider and who the deployer? Does its output reach the EU? Write 4-5 sentences justifying your classification.

stops.title: Banned practices (Article 5)
stops.contentMd:
Bans have applied since 2 Feb 2025. Fines go up to **35m euro or 7% of global turnover**, whichever is higher.

**Why ban instead of control?** With a high-risk system, harm comes from the AI *failing* (bias, errors), and controls can fix that. With a banned practice, harm comes from the AI *working exactly as designed*. No control can fix a purpose that is itself the harm.

| Article | Banned | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5(1)(a) | Subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques that materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm | Takes away free choice |
| 5(1)(b) | Exploiting vulnerability from age, disability or social/economic situation | Targets those least able to resist |
| 5(1)(c) | Social scoring leading to unjustified or disproportionate bad treatment | Punishes people for unrelated things |
| 5(1)(d) | Predicting an individual will commit a crime based only on profiling or personality | Punishes who you are, not what you did |
| 5(1)(e) | Untargeted scraping of face images to build recognition databases | Mass surveillance without consent |
| 5(1)(f) | Emotion recognition in workplaces and education (medical/safety excepted) | Power imbalance, weak science |
| 5(1)(g) | Biometric categorisation inferring race, political views, union membership, religion, sex life or orientation | Enables discrimination on sensitive traits |
| 5(1)(h) | Real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces by police | Chills public life |
| New (Dec 2026) | AI generating non-consensual intimate imagery or CSAM ("nudifier" apps) | Added by the 2026 Omnibus |

**The one ban with exceptions: 5(1)(h).** Police may use live face recognition to search for abduction/trafficking victims, prevent an imminent threat to life or a terror attack, or locate suspects of serious crimes — only with prior judicial or independent authorisation.

**Advanced point.** Each ban has precise conditions, so classification is a legal test, not a label. Emotion recognition on *customers* is not banned (only workplaces and education are), but it is high-risk.

quiz.question: What is the maximum fine for a banned practice under the EU AI Act?
quiz.answer: 35 million euro or 7% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.
quiz.explanation: This is the Act's highest penalty tier — reserved for the 9 banned practices in Article 5.

quiz.question: Why are some AI practices banned outright instead of just being classified high-risk and controlled?
quiz.answer: Because the harm comes from the AI working exactly as designed, not from it failing — so no control (testing, oversight, logging) can fix a purpose that is itself the harm.
quiz.explanation: This is the key distinction between Article 5 (banned) and Article 6 (high-risk, controllable).

stops.artifactPrompt: A client wants to deploy an AI tool that scores call-centre agents on emotional state detected from voice tone, for performance management. Write a 1-paragraph advisory memo: is this banned, high-risk, or neither, and why? Cite the specific Article 5 provision if it applies.

stops.title: High-risk AI: classification and duties
stops.contentMd:
This is the core of the Act. High-risk AI is allowed, but only after it's proven safe, and it must stay supervised.

## Step 1: Is it high-risk? (Article 6)

Two doors in. **Door 1, Annex I (products):** the AI is a product, or a safety part of one, already covered by EU product law (toys, medical devices, machinery, lifts, cars) needing a third-party safety check. **Door 2, Annex III (eight areas of life):**

| # | Area | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Biometrics | Remote face identification, emotion recognition |
| 2 | Critical infrastructure | AI managing the electricity grid or water supply |
| 3 | Education | AI marking exams or deciding admissions |
| 4 | Employment | CV screening, promotion/firing decisions, monitoring staff |
| 5 | Essential services | Credit scoring, insurance pricing, public benefits, emergency call triage (fraud detection excluded) |
| 6 | Law enforcement | Assessing evidence reliability, victim risk |
| 7 | Migration and borders | Assessing visa or asylum applications |
| 8 | Justice and democracy | Helping judges, influencing elections |

**The escape hatch, Article 6(3).** An Annex III system is *not* high-risk if it poses no significant risk because it only does a narrow procedural task, improves a finished human task, spots patterns without replacing human judgement, or does preparatory work. **But any Annex III system that profiles people is always high-risk.** A provider using this escape hatch must document why and still register the system.

## Step 2: What the provider must do (Articles 9-17)

| Article | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| 9 | Risk management system, for the whole lifecycle |
| 10 | Data governance: quality, representativeness, bias checks |
| 11 + Annex IV | Technical documentation |
| 12 | Automatic logging |
| 13 | Instructions for use for the deployer |
| 14 | Human oversight: a person can understand, override, stop it |
| 15 | Accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity |
| 17 | Quality management system |

Then: conformity assessment (Article 43), EU declaration of conformity (47), CE mark (48), registration in the EU database (49), post-market monitoring (72), serious incident reporting (73).

## Step 3: What the deployer must do (Articles 26-27)

Use it as instructed; assign trained people to oversee it; ensure input data is relevant; monitor and report risks and serious incidents; keep logs at least six months; tell workers and affected people when it's used on them. **Fundamental rights impact assessment (Article 27)** before use, if you are a public body, a private body providing public services, or using it for credit scoring or life/health insurance pricing.

**Advanced points:** a deployer that substantially modifies a high-risk system, changes its purpose, or puts its own name on it becomes the provider (Article 25). A person affected by a high-risk decision with significant effects can ask for an explanation (Article 86, right to explanation).

quiz.question: Name the two ways ("doors") a system becomes high-risk under Article 6.
quiz.answer: Door 1: it's a product (or safety component) already covered by EU product law needing third-party safety checks (Annex I). Door 2: it falls into one of the eight Annex III areas of life (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, justice/democracy).
quiz.explanation: Classification always starts here before anything else.

quiz.question: Name three duties a high-risk AI provider must meet under Articles 9-17.
quiz.answer: Any three of: risk management system, data governance/bias checks, technical documentation, automatic logging, instructions for use, human oversight design, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity testing, quality management system.
quiz.explanation: These map to the car-safety analogy: it's the full pre-sale engineering and testing regime.

stops.artifactPrompt: Take a CV-screening AI tool used by an HR department. Walk through the full classification: (1) is it an AI system, (2) which Annex III area does it fall under, (3) does the Article 6(3) escape hatch apply, (4) list 3 specific provider duties and 2 specific deployer duties that would apply. Write this as a one-page classification memo.

stops.title: Transparency duties and general-purpose AI models
stops.contentMd:
## Transparency obligations (Article 50, applies from 2 Aug 2026)

The splash-pool sign: you can use it, but people must be told. These duties can apply on top of high-risk duties.

| Duty | Who | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tell people they're talking to AI, unless obvious | Provider | A bank's customer chatbot says "I'm an AI assistant" |
| Mark AI-generated audio, images, video and text in a machine-readable way | Provider of generative AI | Invisible watermark in generated images |
| Inform people exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation | Deployer | Call centre tells customers voice analytics is in use |
| Disclose deepfakes, and AI-generated text published to inform the public | Deployer | A label on a synthetic video |

The 2026 Omnibus gave generative systems already on the market before 2 Aug 2026 until 2 Dec 2026 to add watermarking. New systems get no grace period.

## General-purpose AI models (Articles 51-56, applied from 2 Aug 2025)

**Why this was added late:** the original 2021 draft regulated AI by use. Then ChatGPT showed one model can serve thousands of uses, so lawmakers added rules at the **model** level, upstream of every use — like checking the flour at the factory, not only each cake.

**All GPAI providers (Article 53):** technical documentation; information for downstream providers building on the model; a copyright compliance policy; a public summary of training content. Free open-source models are partly exempt.

**GPAI with systemic risk (Articles 51, 55):** presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs, or designated by the Commission. Extra duties: model evaluations including adversarial testing, assessing and mitigating systemic risks, serious incident reporting, cybersecurity.

**Code of Practice (July 2025):** the voluntary route for providers to show compliance. Fines for GPAI providers: up to 15m euro or 3%, enforceable from Aug 2026.

**Advanced point.** A bank building a chatbot on a third-party model is not the GPAI provider — it is the provider (or deployer) of the *AI system* built on top, and relies on the model provider's Article 53 information.

quiz.question: Why did the EU AI Act add separate rules for general-purpose AI (GPAI) models at the model level, rather than regulating only by use case?
quiz.answer: Because ChatGPT showed that one model can serve thousands of different downstream uses, breaking the original 'risk by use' logic — so lawmakers added upstream obligations on the model itself (Articles 51-56), like checking flour at the factory rather than every cake made from it.
quiz.explanation: This is why GPAI rules were a late addition (Dec 2023) to the original 2021 draft.

quiz.question: What training compute threshold creates a presumption of 'systemic risk' for a GPAI model?
quiz.answer: 10^25 FLOPs of training compute (or designation by the European Commission).
quiz.explanation: Systemic-risk GPAI providers face extra duties: adversarial testing, systemic risk mitigation, incident reporting, cybersecurity.

stops.artifactPrompt: A company builds a customer-support chatbot on top of a third-party foundation model. List which Article 50 transparency duties apply to the chatbot, and explain why the company is not the GPAI provider under Article 53 even though it customizes the model's behavior.

stops.title: Enforcement, timeline, and how it connects to other rules
stops.contentMd:
## Who enforces it

| Body | Role |
| --- | --- |
| AI Office (inside the European Commission) | Supervises GPAI models; after the Omnibus, also AI systems built by the same provider on its own GPAI model |
| AI Board | Member-state representatives; keeps application consistent across the EU |
| National market surveillance authorities | Enforce on the ground: inspections, fines, withdrawing systems. Financial-sector AI stays with financial supervisors |
| Notified bodies | Independent checkers for conformity assessments that need a third party |

## Penalties (Article 99)

| Breach | Maximum fine |
| --- | --- |
| Banned practices | 35m euro or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher |
| Most other obligations (high-risk, transparency) | 15m euro or 3% |
| Incorrect or misleading information to authorities | 7.5m euro or 1% |

For SMEs and start-ups, the *lower* of the two amounts applies.

## Timeline

Annex III (credit scoring, hiring, insurance pricing) is the date most clients plan around. **The 2026 Digital Omnibus** delayed the high-risk dates because harmonised standards (written by CEN-CENELEC JTC 21) and Commission guidance weren't ready. It also softened AI literacy (Article 4) to "support the development of" literacy, added the nudifier ban, extended bias-detection data processing to all AI systems, and pushed national sandboxes to Aug 2027. Bans, GPAI duties and Article 50 did not move.

## How it connects to other rules

- **GDPR still applies in full.** The AI Act regulates the AI system; GDPR regulates the personal data inside it. A fundamental rights impact assessment can build on an existing DPIA.
- **Harmonised standards.** Once published, following them gives a "presumption of conformity" — the easiest way to prove compliance.
- **ISO/IEC 42001** supports the quality management system (Article 17) but does not equal AI Act compliance — the Act has product-level duties 42001 doesn't cover.
- **Sandboxes (Article 57) and real-world testing (Article 60)** let firms test AI under regulator supervision before full compliance.
- **Sector law stays.** Banks still answer to financial regulators; the Omnibus lets the Commission limit AI Act duties that duplicate sector rules.

quiz.question: What are the three penalty tiers under Article 99, and which breach triggers the highest one?
quiz.answer: 35m euro/7% for banned practices (highest); 15m euro/3% for most other obligations including high-risk and transparency; 7.5m euro/1% for giving incorrect/misleading information to authorities. SMEs and start-ups get the lower of the two amounts in each tier.
quiz.explanation: Penalty tier always tracks the severity logic: banned practices (unfixable harm) get the harshest fines.

quiz.question: What did the 2026 Digital Omnibus change, and what did it leave untouched?
quiz.answer: It delayed the high-risk (Annex III/I) compliance dates because harmonised standards weren't ready, softened the AI literacy requirement, added a ban on 'nudifier' apps, extended bias-detection data processing rules, and pushed sandbox deadlines to 2027. It left banned practices, GPAI duties, and Article 50 transparency obligations unchanged.
quiz.explanation: This is a common 'what changed in 2026' interview question — know what moved and what didn't.

stops.artifactPrompt: Write a short timeline briefing (5-6 bullet points) explaining to a non-technical stakeholder which EU AI Act obligations are already in force today versus which were delayed by the 2026 Digital Omnibus, and why the delay happened.

stops.title: Worked example: classifying LoanLeaf's two AI tools
stops.contentMd:
LoanLeaf, a fictional EU lender in Ireland, wants two AI tools: a credit-scoring model bought from a vendor (ScoreCo), and a customer chatbot built in-house on a third-party LLM.

### Tool 1: the credit-scoring model

1. **Is it an AI system?** Yes — it learned from past loans to infer default risk.
2. **Banned?** No — it doesn't manipulate, social-score, or use sensitive biometric traits.
3. **High-risk?** Yes — creditworthiness evaluation is Annex III point 5(b). The 6(3) escape hatch fails because it profiles individuals.
4. **Roles.** ScoreCo is the provider; LoanLeaf is the deployer.
5. **ScoreCo must:** run a risk management system, prove data quality and bias checks, write technical documentation, build in logging and human-override features, pass a conformity assessment, CE-mark it, register it, and give LoanLeaf instructions for use.
6. **LoanLeaf must:** complete a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use (credit scoring triggers Article 27), follow the instructions, assign trained underwriters to oversee decisions, keep logs at least six months, monitor and report serious incidents, tell applicants AI is used, and explain decisions on request (Article 86).
7. **The trap.** If LoanLeaf's data team retrains ScoreCo's model on LoanLeaf's own data, that may be a substantial modification, making LoanLeaf the provider (Article 25) with all of ScoreCo's duties.
8. **When.** From 2 Dec 2027 — starting now still leaves only about a year to build the evidence.

### Tool 2: the customer chatbot

1. **High-risk?** No, as long as it only answers questions and doesn't decide credit.
2. **Transparency.** Yes — it must tell customers they're talking to AI (Article 50, already in force).
3. **GPAI.** LoanLeaf is not the GPAI provider; it relies on the model provider's Article 53 documentation.
4. **Scope creep.** If the chatbot later pre-approves loans, it becomes high-risk. The AI inventory must flag purpose changes.

### What a consultant would deliver

An inventory with each system's role and tier, a gap analysis against the obligations, an FRIA template, contract clauses for ScoreCo (documentation, logs, change notice), an oversight procedure for underwriters, and a roadmap to Dec 2027.
stops.artifactPrompt: Pick two real or hypothetical AI tools from your own experience or target industry. Run them through the same 8-point classification LoanLeaf's credit-scoring tool went through above: AI system?, banned?, high-risk?, roles, provider duties, deployer duties, the retraining/modification trap, and the compliance deadline. Write this as a one-page worked example you could show in an interview.

stops.title: Interview questions and self-check
stops.contentMd:
## Interview questions

| Question | Crisp answer |
| --- | --- |
| Explain the EU AI Act in 10 seconds | A risk-based EU law that sorts AI by the harm its use can cause: banned, high-risk, transparency, minimal, with heavier rules the higher the tier. |
| Why is it risk-based? | Regulating all AI equally would either crush harmless tools or miss dangerous ones. Proportionality aims the effort where people can be hurt. |
| Why are some practices banned outright? | Their harm comes from the AI working as designed, so no control can fix it. |
| How do you classify a system? | Is it an AI system? Banned under Art 5? High-risk via Annex I or III, after the 6(3) test? Transparency duties under Art 50? Otherwise minimal. Then decide provider or deployer. |
| Provider vs deployer? | Provider builds/brands it and carries product duties (Arts 9-17, conformity, CE). Deployer uses it: oversight, logs, monitoring, FRIA for credit/insurance. |
| A client wants to keep a prohibited use case — what do you advise? | Confirm the exact Article 5 conditions are met. If they are, there's no compliance route: redesign the purpose, population or data, or keep it out of the EU. Renaming isn't redesign. |
| What changed in 2026? | The Digital Omnibus delayed Annex III to Dec 2027 and Annex I to Aug 2028, added a nudifier ban, softened AI literacy. Bans, GPAI and Art 50 didn't move. |
| Does ISO 42001 make you AI Act compliant? | No. It supports the quality management system in Art 17, but the Act has product-level duties 42001 doesn't cover. |

## Self-check

Answer out loud before reading the answers.

1. A US company scores EU job applicants with AI from its US office. In scope?
2. A call centre detects customer frustration from voice tone. Banned, high-risk or minimal?
3. The same tool monitors call-centre staff performance. Now?
4. Name three things a deployer of a high-risk system must do.
5. A bank fine-tunes a vendor's credit model on its own data. What's the risk?
6. What does training compute above 10^25 FLOPs trigger?
7. Maximum fine for a banned practice?

**Answers:** (1) Yes, the output is used in the EU. (2) High-risk: emotion recognition from biometric data, Annex III 1(c), plus Art 50(3) disclosure. (3) Banned, Art 5(1)(f), emotion recognition at work. (4) Any three of: follow instructions, human oversight, relevant input data, monitor and report, keep logs 6 months, inform workers and affected people, FRIA where required. (5) A substantial modification could make the bank the provider (Art 25). (6) Presumption of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk (Art 51). (7) 35m euro or 7% of global turnover, whichever is higher.

quiz.question: A client's tool classifies loan applicants as high, medium, or low risk and this classification is advisory only — a human underwriter makes the final call. Does the Article 6(3) escape hatch apply?
quiz.answer: No — any Annex III system that profiles individuals is always high-risk regardless of the escape hatch, and credit scoring is explicitly Annex III point 5(b). The human-in-the-loop detail doesn't change the classification, though it is relevant to the human oversight duty (Article 14) once classified high-risk.
quiz.explanation: This tests whether the learner understands that profiling overrides the 6(3) escape hatch — a common interview trap.

stops.artifactPrompt: Write out your own 60-second answer to "Walk me through how you'd classify an AI system under the EU AI Act," using the question list above as a checklist. Practice saying it out loud and time yourself — aim for under 60 seconds.
